papers.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper introduces an agentic AI system that can infer cell types directly from spatial transcriptomics data without needing prior cell segmentation. The same AI framework then uses these inferred cell types to guide and improve the accuracy of cell segmentation itself. This reverses the typical workflow where segmentation must happen before cell typing, potentially solving a major bottleneck in spatial transcriptomics analysis.
papers.why: This method could substantially improve how you analyze spatial transcriptomics data in brain tissue, especially for accurately identifying interneuron subtypes without the segmentation errors common in densely packed neuronal regions.
papers.figure: A figure showing a workflow comparison between traditional segmentation-first versus the new segmentation-free cell-type inference pipeline, likely with example outputs on brain tissue sections.

papers.title: A Damage-Gated Small-Molecule Chimera Selectively Enhances Mitophagy by Coupling Dysfunctional Mitochondria to Autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper describes a small-molecule chimera designed to selectively target damaged, dysfunctional mitochondria and link them to the cell's autophagy machinery. Unlike general mitophagy inducers, this molecule is 'damage-gated,' meaning it preferentially acts on mitochondria that are already impaired, sparing healthy ones. The approach aims to enhance clearance of faulty mitochondria without disrupting normal mitochondrial function or bulk autophagy.
papers.why: This chimera offers a potential pharmacological tool to selectively induce mitophagy of damaged mitochondria in neurons, which could be tested in brain tissue alongside spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic readouts to study how targeted mitochondrial quality control affects interneuron health and perineuronal net integrity.
papers.figure: Figure showing the chimera's mechanism of selective binding to damaged mitochondria versus healthy mitochondria, likely including dose-response or selectivity data comparing mitophagy flux in damaged vs. healthy mitochondrial populations.

papers.title: Protocol for reference-free single-cell-resolution deconvolution of spot-based spatial transcriptomics with CoexpressDeconvolve.
papers.summary: This paper presents a step-by-step protocol for a computational method called CoexpressDeconvolve, which breaks down spot-based spatial transcriptomics data into single-cell-resolution information without needing a pre-existing reference dataset. It works by leveraging gene co-expression patterns within spots to infer individual cell identities and locations. This reference-free approach could make spatial transcriptomics analysis more accessible and accurate, especially for tissues or cell types lacking well-characterized reference atlases.
papers.why: This protocol could enable higher-resolution spatial transcriptomic mapping of interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated gene expression without requiring pre-existing single-cell reference datasets, which are often incomplete for specialized neuronal niches.

papers.title: ZeXieYin formula attenuates trimethylamine N-oxide- induced atherosclerosis and cognitive impairment by regulating microglial-neuronal signaling and autophagy.
papers.summary: This study investigates a traditional Chinese medicine formula called ZeXieYin and its effects on atherosclerosis and cognitive decline caused by trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a gut microbiome-derived metabolite. The researchers found that this formula works by influencing communication between microglia (brain immune cells) and neurons, as well as by modulating autophagy processes. The findings suggest a potential therapeutic approach for conditions linking vascular disease to cognitive impairment through neuroinflammatory and autophagic mechanisms.
papers.why: This paper touches on autophagy regulation in neurons and microglial-neuronal signaling, which is directly relevant to the mechanistic focus of the PhD project, though it lacks the spatial transcriptomics, interneuron, or perineuronal net components central to the profile.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagy markers (e.g., LC3, p62) in neurons alongside microglial activation markers in brain tissue sections from TMAO-treated versus ZeXieYin-treated animals.

papers.title: Puerarin preserves microglial homeostasis and protects against acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating autophagy and oxidative stress through Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3.
papers.summary: This study investigates how puerarin, a natural plant compound, affects microglia (the brain's immune cells) during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, which occurs when blood flow returns to brain tissue after a stroke. The researchers found that puerarin helps maintain normal microglial function and reduces injury by influencing autophagy (cellular self-cleaning processes) and oxidative stress levels. These effects were linked to the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway, a well-known cellular communication route involved in inflammation and stress responses.
papers.why: While this paper centers on microglia rather than neurons or interneurons, it offers relevant mechanistic insight into autophagy regulation and oxidative stress signaling in brain injury, which could inform comparative analyses of autophagy pathways across different brain cell types in the PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagy markers (e.g., LC3, p62) and oxidative stress indicators in microglia across treatment groups, correlated with JAK2/STAT3 pathway activity.

papers.title: Spatially Resolved Immunometabolic Reprogramming of Tumor-Associated Macrophages: An Integrative Multi-Layer Re-Analysis of Public Spatial Metabolomics, Spatial Transcriptomics and Single-Cell Resources
papers.summary: This paper re-analyzes existing public datasets combining spatial metabolomics, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell data to study how tumor-associated macrophages change their metabolic programs based on their location within tumors. It integrates multiple data layers to map spatial patterns of immune cell metabolism in the tumor microenvironment. The work is a methodological and conceptual demonstration of multi-omic spatial data integration rather than new experimental data generation.
papers.why: This paper's cross-platform integration strategy for combining spatial metabolomics with spatial transcriptomics and single-cell data offers a transferable analytical framework that could be adapted to study neuronal/glial metabolic states and perineuronal net microenvironments in brain tissue.

papers.title: Exercise-induced lactylation in WDR41 initiates autophagy and improves fatty liver diseases.
papers.summary: This study finds that exercise increases a chemical modification called lactylation on a protein called WDR41. This modification triggers autophagy, the cell's process for clearing out damaged components. The researchers show this pathway helps improve fatty liver disease, likely by boosting the liver's ability to break down excess fat through autophagic mechanisms.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on liver rather than brain tissue, it offers a mechanistic model of lactylation-driven autophagy initiation via WDR41 that could inform how similar post-translational modifications might regulate mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurons.
papers.figure: Figure showing the proposed mechanism linking WDR41 lactylation to autophagy initiation and downstream effects on lipid clearance

papers.title: KRT8 activates mitophagy to preserves chondrocyte apoptosis and extracellular matrix degradation in osteoarthritis: A PPARγ-mediated mechanism.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the protein KRT8 influences chondrocyte (cartilage cell) biology in osteoarthritis. It reports that KRT8 activates mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, and that this affects chondrocyte apoptosis and breakdown of the extracellular matrix. The authors propose PPARγ signaling as the mechanistic link connecting KRT8 to these mitophagy-related outcomes.
papers.why: While this study centers on cartilage rather than brain tissue, it offers a potential mechanistic parallel for mitophagy regulation via PPARγ signaling that could inform how similar pathways might operate in neurons or glia.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed KRT8-PPARγ-mitophagy signaling pathway with its downstream effects on chondrocyte apoptosis and extracellular matrix degradation.
